results.title: How to Ensure Representativeness in Your Research Sample
results.content: # What are the best ways to ensure your sample is representative? It means that your sample reflects the characteristics and diversity of the population you want to study. A representative sample can help you avoid bias, generalize your findings, and increase your credibility. But how can you ensure that your sample is representative? I follow the United Nations Economic and Social Council's (ECOSOC) approach to ensuring sample representativeness, which involves clearly defining the target population. This precision helps in selecting a sample that accurately mirrors the diversity within the larger population, ensuring that the findings are both meaningful and applicable on a broader scale. Probability sampling means that every element in your population has a known and equal chance of being selected for your sample. I admire the United Nations' approach to ensuring representative samples through stratified random sampling. The third step is to calculate your sample size based on your sampling method, confidence level, margin of error, and population variance. A larger sample size can help you reduce sampling error and increase representativeness, but it may also increase costs and complexity. We should calculate our sample size meticulously to ensure it is representative of the population. Utilizing statistical methods such as random sampling and stratified sampling helps minimize biases and ensures diverse inclusion. By employing rigorous sampling techniques, like stratification based on geographical regions and demographic characteristics, the UNFPA ensures that its collected data accurately reflects the diverse perspectives and needs of populations worldwide, enhancing the reliability and applicability of their findings. A high response rate can help you ensure that your sample is representative and complete, but it may require more effort and incentives. We should monitor our response rate to ensure our sample is representative. By tracking and analyzing response rates, we can identify and address potential biases, ensuring a more accurate reflection of the diverse viewpoints within the surveyed population. The final step is to check your sample characteristics against your population characteristics. results.title: National Academies Report: Research Equity in Clinical Trials Can Save Lives and Money | Published by Journal of Health Economics and Outcomes Research
results.content:
Title: National Academies Report: Research Equity in Clinical Trials Can Save Lives and Money | Published by Journal of Health Economics and Outcomes Research
## RSS Feed. Enter the URL below into your favorite RSS reader. # National Academies Report: Research Equity in Clinical Trials Can Save Lives and Money. Underrepresentation of minority and other populations in clinical trials and research is widening the gap in health outcomes and imposing an enormous economic toll on the US, according to a new study report from the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM). * Sexual and gender minority (SGM) populations. * Hinders innovation and discovery of variations and new biological processes. * Widens health disparities in underrepresented groups and hinders health equity. The study report estimated the life expectancy, disability-free life expectancy, and working years gained if disparities were eliminated for three common chronic conditions. For example, eliminating disparities for heart disease among Hispanics, non-Hispanic Blacks, and non-Hispanic women would result in a nearly one-year increase in life expectancy, over a one-year increase in disability-free life years, and a half-year increase in years in the workforce. # Barriers to Inclusive Research. Barriers can also be “baked into” the clinical research process itself. * Intention and agency to achieve representativeness: Invest time and establish relationships. * A foundation of trust with participants and the larger community. * Resources and support to achieve representativeness. Photo by CDC on Unsplash. # Recommendations and Opportunities for Improvement. The study report concludes with a case for investment in improving representation and offers the following recommendations, including:. * The FDA should require study sponsors to submit a recruitment plan explaining in detail how they will ensure that the trial population will adequately reflect the disease demographics. * FDA should be authorized to enforce accountability measures and directed to establish a task force to study incentives for achieving representative trials. * The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) should incentivize community providers to enroll participants in clinical trials by reimbursing for time and infrastructure. * The Government Accountability Office should assess the impact of reimbursing routine care costs associated with clinical trial participation through Medicare and Medicaid. * Clinical research sponsors should ensure adequate compensation for research participants. results.title: Recruitment Strategies to Optimize Participation by Diverse Populations
results.content: We recommend SEM researchers should build an equitable, diverse and inclusive research team and include community members; apply a multilevel, intersectional framework; minimise and acknowledge potential biases in the study design and incorporate qualitative or mixed-methods approaches if appropriate; apply multiple inclusive strategies for recruiting and retaining diverse populations; collect accurate and representative data using inclusive data collection methods and tools with validity and reliability in the populations of interest; apply measures with evidence of validity and reliability in the populations of interest; implement a data analysis plan that reflects the conceptual and theoretical frameworks; and promote broad dissemination and interventions that ultimately address and reduce health inequities. Despite having a broad sampling frame which included targeted efforts to recruit diverse clinicians in this study, recruitment of diverse populations continues to be an identified challenge in clinical research (e.g.,Webber-Ritchey et al., 2021).Research demonstrates that most clinicians within the health service workforce in Western nations such as the USA identify as White (88%;Lin et al., 2018); therefore, it is possible that our sample characteristics simply represent the existing demographic of mental health clinicians within the field-albeit raising the broader issue of a lack of diversity of clinicians in EDs. Given this, it is imperative to recruit and train diverse clinicians to provide FBT to a broad range of diverse families seen in clinical practice.In conclusion, including clinician perspectives on their implementation of FBT with diverse families will allow ED researchers and providers to examine whether broader adaptations to the model areneeded to accommodate diverse family systems, as well as how individualized care in FBT can be improved upon to ensure that variations to the model remain fidelity-consistent (Wiltsey Stirman et al., 2019) and meet the unique needs of all families in practice. Additional recommendations to increase the participation of women of color in future research studies include building a diverse research team, developing culturally sensitive recruitment materials, and identifying key community contacts (Shavers et al., 2002;Webber-Ritchey et al., 2021). Greater comparative understanding of barriers and facilitators to racial/ethnic minorities’ research participation can improve population-specific recruitment and retention strategies and could better inform future large-scale prospective quantitative and in-depth ethnographic studies.

In this article, we'll offer advice for building a recruitment process that promotes diversity, equity, and inclusion, and explain why it's so important. Why Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion are Important in Hiring Diversity, equity, and inclusion are crucial components of a successful business. Tips for Creating a Diverse and Inclusive Hiring Process 1. Define what diversity, equity, and inclusion mean for your organisation: Before you begin creating a diverse and inclusive hiring process, it's important to define what these terms mean for your organisation. Consider what diversity means in the context of your industry and customer base, and how you can ensure that your hiring process is equitable and inclusive. 2. Evaluate your current hiring process: Take a close look at your current hiring process and identify any areas where diversity, equity, or inclusion may be lacking. Creating a diverse and inclusive hiring process is essential for building a successful business. By promoting diversity, equity, and inclusion in your recruitment efforts, you can ensure that your organisation is better equipped to understand and serve a diverse customer base, and promote a welcoming and inclusive environment for all employees. By following the tips outlined in this article, you can create a hiring process that promotes diversity, equity, and inclusion. Remember, building a diverse and inclusive team is an ongoing effort, and it's important to continue to evaluate and improve your hiring process over time. By making diversity, equity, and inclusion a priority in your recruitment efforts, you can help ensure that your business is successful and that all employees feel valued and respected. **How can I measure my progress towards diversity, equity, and inclusion goals?** You can measure your progress by tracking the demographics of your applicant pool, interviewees, and new hires over time.

results.title: 6. Performance Incentives that Align with Equity Priorities
results.content: If performance incentives are designed to encourage energy equity, program implementers will deliver more programs to historically marginalized and/or excluded communities. Ensuring procedural equity means that community members “define, drive, and hold accountable clean energy policy and program decisions and outcomes.” Performance incentives that encourage procedural equity will encourage program implementers to engage with and incorporate feedback from historically marginalized and/or excluded communities for both program design and workforce efforts. 3 Distributional Equity Performance Incentives Distributional equity performance incentives can encourage program implementers to design programs that prioritize historically marginalized and/or excluded communities because they require that all customers receive the benefits of energy efficiency programs. Performance incentives to encourage structural equity will ensure equal access to the benefits of energy efficiency programs and proactively remove barriers that have prevented participation by historically marginalized and/or excluded communities.
